explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Metheg-ammah from their hand (2 Samuel 8:1). It's the first win on a list that gets long in a hurry. I'd need a second apron just to keep count.

Not the Midianites, friend. Verse 1 says David defeated the Philistines and took Metheg-ammah from their hand. The Midianites never show up anywhere in this passage. A list this fast will make anybody grab for a familiar name, and I've grabbed a hot pan bare-handed for less.

The Hittites aren't in this passage, friend. Verse 1 has David defeating the Philistines and taking Metheg-ammah from their hand. The very first line of the list names them. Once you've got that one, the rest of the list gets easier to follow.

Spared is right. Two lengths of the cord were for those to be put to death, and one length was for those to be spared (2 Samuel 8:2). This is a heavy moment, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there. The one-length group is the group that was spared.

The verse doesn't say exiled, friend. It says two lengths were for those to be put to death, and one length was for those to be spared (2 Samuel 8:2). Nothing about sending anyone away. It's a heavy verse, so I'll stick to exactly what it says.

Branded isn't in the verse, baker. The text says two lengths marked those to be put to death, and one length marked those to be spared (2 Samuel 8:2). That's a heavy part of the passage, and the word that fits is spared.

Tribute, yes. The Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute (2 Samuel 8:2). Tribute is a payment made by people who are under someone's rule. So the verse tells you who they answer to and what they bring.

Chariots come up in verse 4, friend, and those are chariots David captures from Hadadezer, king of Zobah. The Moabites in verse 2 bring tribute. Same passage, different crowd. Chariots are a lot to carry in a bag anyway.

Soldiers show up in verse 4, baker, and those are soldiers David captures from Hadadezer, king of Zobah. The Moabites in verse 2 become subject to David and bring tribute. Nobody in that verse is delivering troops.
The Euphrates, yes. Hadadezer had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River (2 Samuel 8:3). Big river, big plans. David defeated him anyway.

The Jordan isn't the river in this verse, friend. The text says Hadadezer marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River (2 Samuel 8:3). The Jordan is a famous name, so I understand the grab. This verse points to the Euphrates.

The Nile doesn't come up here, baker. Verse 3 says Hadadezer had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River. It's a famous river, so it's an easy one to reach for. The Euphrates is the one in this verse.

Not quite, friend. David hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots (2 Samuel 8:4). So he kept a hundred, not every one. This is a hard detail, so I'll just give it as the text gives it.

False is right. The text says David hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots (2 Samuel 8:4). So he kept only a hundred of them. It's a tough detail, and the verse gives it plainly.

That's them. The Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, and David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men (2 Samuel 8:5). Backup showed up, and the backup needed backup. Then in verse 6 the Arameans became subject to David.

Not this time, friend. The helpers in verse 5 are the Arameans of Damascus. The Ammonites only show up later, in verse 12, in the list of nations whose silver and gold David dedicated. Same passage, different spot in the list.

The Amalekites aren't the helpers here, baker. Verse 5 says the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah. The Amalekites only appear in verse 12, in the list of nations whose silver and gold David dedicated.

The LORD, yes. The passage says, “So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.” (2 Samuel 8:6). It says it right after the garrisons and the tribute. All those wins, and the passage gives the credit to Him.

Joab is in this passage, friend. He's Joab son of Zeruiah, over the army, in the list of officials at the end (2 Samuel 8:16). But verse 6 gives the credit somewhere else: “So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.” The passage names the LORD as the One who made David victorious.

Mighty men don't come up in this passage, baker. Verse 6 says, “So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.” The text puts the LORD in the spot where you'd expect a list of fighters. It's worth noticing who the passage names.

Jerusalem is right. David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:7). That's a lot of gold on the road. I'd have been checking the cargo every five minutes.
Hebron never comes up in this passage, friend. Verse 7 says David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem. That's the city the verse names.
Gibeon isn't in this passage, baker. The text says David brought the gold shields of Hadadezer's officers to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:7). The destination is right there in the verse.

His son Joram, yes. King Toi of Hamath sent Joram to greet King David and bless him for defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi (2 Samuel 8:10). Joram came carrying articles of silver and gold and bronze. That's quite a greeting.
Hanun isn't the one in this passage, friend. Verse 10 says King Toi of Hamath sent his son Joram to greet David. Joram brought articles of silver and gold and bronze with him.
Abner doesn't appear in this passage, baker. Toi, king of Hamath, sent his own son Joram to greet King David (2 Samuel 8:10). Joram came with articles of silver and gold and bronze.

True. King David dedicated these gifts to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued (2 Samuel 8:11). The gifts from Toi's son went right into that dedicated pile. Verse 12 then lists where the rest came from.

The text says otherwise, friend. “…King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued—” (2 Samuel 8:11). So the gifts from Joram were dedicated to the LORD. The answer is True.

A name, baker. “And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.” (2 Samuel 8:13). The verse says exactly that. It puts the name right at the homecoming.

No palace in this verse, friend. It says David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt (2 Samuel 8:13). The thing he made was a name. A palace would be a lot to build on the way home anyway.

A treaty isn't mentioned here, baker. Verse 13 says David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The passage says a name, so that's the answer.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David.” (2 Samuel 8:14). That's all the Edomites, not just some. So the statement is False.
False is right. Verse 14 says, “He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David.” (2 Samuel 8:14). The word is all. No Edomites are left out in that verse.

That's the one, friend. The passage says David “…administered justice and righteousness for all his people” (2 Samuel 8:15). After all the battles, this verse tells how he ruled. It's a quiet line after a loud chapter.

Strength and fear aren't the words in this verse, baker. It says David “…administered justice and righteousness for all his people” (2 Samuel 8:15). The passage uses those two words for how he ruled all Israel.

There's plenty of gold and bronze in this chapter, friend, but verse 15 doesn't use those words for how David ruled. It says he “…administered justice and righteousness for all his people” (2 Samuel 8:15). Justice and righteousness are the two the passage names.
